body.text: Author Trent Dalton's youthful diaries helped singer Katie Noonan remember the power of love
As ARIA award-winning singer Katie Noonan sat in the audience watching author Trent Dalton's book Love Stories coming to life on stage, her own love story was falling apart.
That day, Katie found out that the 26-year partnership with her jazz saxophonist husband and father of her two children was all but over.

"I remember that day so vividly," Katie, 49, tells Australian Story. "It was quite intense actually, watching that play and the searing honesty of how hard [it is] in the trenches, being married and being artists."
After the show, Katie bumped into Trent, the author of the international bestseller Boy Swallows Universe, and his wife and co-writer of the play, Fiona Franzmann.

Katie and Trent had known each other since 2001, when they were enthusiastic young creatives from Brisbane; he was a fledgling journalist who had come to interview her, the breakout star with the ethereal voice from the indie pop rock band named george.
Now, as they caught up over a drink, Katie told Trent how much the play had touched her. How beautiful the writing was and how real it felt.
And that her own marriage was in serious trouble.
"She really let me know she was going through one of the toughest times in her life," Trent recalls. "And that was where my relationship with Katie kind of got a bit more poignant."
Six weeks later, Katie was out of the family home and living alone in a new place on Queensland's Sunshine Coast.
"There have been days that were catastrophically hard and dark and lonely and depressed and all those things," Katie says.
But music has always been her best friend, and so she turned to it.

Exploring different music genres is a hallmark of Katie's career. One of her projects is the Australian Vocal Ensemble [AVE], an a capella quartet that celebrates the work of Australian writers such as Tim Winton and the late David Malouf.
She knew Trent and his writing would be perfect as AVE's next muse. "I reached out to him and said, 'Do you have any words?'"
He had plenty. He had 153 pages of thoughts, lyrics and dreams he wrote as a lovesick young man falling for Fiona. He said Katie could have them.
The result was not just a new piece for AVE but an album about love — the wonder and the heartache — and a creative outlet that has helped Katie on the road to healing.
'Bravery and lunacy': Music her way

Growing up, music filled the Noonan household. Katie's mother, Maggie, was an acclaimed opera singer and singing teacher and her late journalist dad, Brian, had been a crooner on shows such as Bandstand.
"One of my fondest memories," Katie says, "[is] sitting in bed with Dad Saturday mornings, listening to ABC Radio, listening to The Goons and the Jazz Show while Mum was teaching."

After leaving school, Katie studied opera at the Queensland Conservatorium of Music (often called The Con) while living in a house "full of thespians, actors and musicians and incense and patchouli oil and a lot of djembes and fire twirling and crystals".
This potent mix led to the formation of the band george (sporting a lower-case g), with Katie's older brother Tyrone on keyboards and guitar.
As Katie explored her musical options, switching to jazz at The Con, the band started touring and building a loyal following.
The 2002 debut album Polyserena reached number one and stayed in the charts for 15 weeks, buoyed by the support of radio stations such as the ABC's triple j and Brisbane community radio station 4ZZZ.
"We were sort of the seven-year overnight success because we'd been touring and touring and touring," Katie says.
By then, Katie had met the man who would become her husband.
"I adored and was madly in love with him," she says.
Within 18 months of marriage, they had two boys, and although Katie's husband played in her next band, Elixir, Katie had the capacity to earn the most.
She became the primary breadwinner, touring widely with a range of bands and different musical genres, while he stayed home to look after the kids.
"As a wife and mother and making so many sacrifices to be the breadwinner, it puts a lot of pressure," Katie's mother Maggie says.

From the outset, Katie was determined to do music her way, without surrendering to commercial interests. When a record company executive told her to lose weight early in her career, she told them "no" in a rather colourful manner.
"I've never been afraid to have an opinion," she says. "I'm always going to speak up for things that matter to me."
Having artistic control in such a fickle industry was so important to Katie that 15 years ago, she started her independent label, an "act of bravery and lunacy in a lot of ways".

It's a tough way to make a living. Albums don't sell in big numbers anymore, she says. And the streaming service Spotify gives very little, if anything, back to artists, a subject Katie has often spoken out about.
So the answer is to tour — and keep touring. "I will play anywhere," she says. "I love playing little, tiny halls … and then I get to play the Opera House."
But when COVID hit, everything went belly-up. Katie was three dates into a 25-day solo tour when the plug was pulled on live gigs. "The financial pressure was staggering," Katie says.
"I put on a lot of weight during COVID … plus a bit of perimenopause rage thrown in," she says. "And, you know, also drinking too much."
There were problems in the marriage before the pandemic, Katie admits, but "COVID broke us".
'I've overshared way too much'
Now, as Katie pulls her solo life together, she acknowledges that separating was the best option, even though she would not have made that decision.
She's desperate for her relationship with her now-adult sons to get back on an even footing but accepts they need time.
"I've stuffed up, I've overshared way too much with them emotionally," she says. "I wish I hadn't in retrospect.
"Being largely estranged from my children has been a sorrow that I wouldn't wish upon anyone, but … they know I love them."
There have been times, Katie says, when she felt she wouldn't get through the day.
On other days, songs just "fell out", demanding to be written. The result was one half of her new album titled Alone but all one.
"It was an album that I never intended to write," she says. "[It] just fell out from a place of deep sadness and sorrow and loss and grief and not knowing who I was anymore."
Amid that torment, she received Trent's 153 pages, his words celebrating "the wonderment" of new love — and a sliver of light entered.
"That was a great gift for me that I needed because I couldn't write those," Katie says. "I was deep in the other world."
Katie Noonan rewrites her ending
Katie is at her piano, singing When the Heart Falls Apart, one of the songs on the new album, while Trent watches on.

Under his elbow is one of his dog-eared notebooks, the pages into which a 20-something Trent poured his joy at having found Fiona — and the pages from which Katie found the words that helped her navigate her marriage breakdown.
The juxtaposition of the joy of love, seen through Trent's eyes, and Katie's heartbreak at its loss is the essence of the album.
It's a thrill for Trent that his "really revealing, really embarrassing" words have found a life outside these pages more than a quarter of a century after writing them.
He's even more chuffed that Katie "took all of that and just turned it into something that might get somewhere close to her feeling better".
"All that gushing I was doing, I think somehow reminded her of the truth — that it was true love," says Trent of Katie's love story with her husband.
"Like any story, the ending shouldn't be the definition of the entire story," he says. "You are allowed to look back on beginnings and middles and go, 'That was amazing.'"
Katie says while the past two years have been the most challenging of her life, she's now at a point of gratitude — for the life she is building and the love she shared with her husband.
"I'll always love him because he's the father of my children and he is a beautiful human and an amazing musician," Katie says.
"I'm so grateful that he allowed me to be an artist because he decided to be a stay-at-home dad. I couldn't have been an artist without him."
Music is her constant. It has been "my succour, my panacea" throughout her heartbreak, she says, and she's immersing herself in it.

For Katie's Australian Vocal Ensemble, a 13-piece song cycle called Just for Dreaming has been created, with music by Jessica Wells and lyrics based on Trent's notebook musings about his hope for a better life after a messy, troubled childhood.
She's heavily involved with the Eumundi School of Music, the "legacy project" she and friends began 10 years ago, providing professional music lessons and scholarships to budding school-age musos.
And Katie Noonan is touring again, singing the songs from the album she never intended to write but, with a little help from a friend, is the one she needed to bring to life.
